prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(InStyle.com) -- It takes a truly adventurous actress to pull off a razored Mohawk, a platinum pixie and a Louise Brooks bob, but we'd expect nothing less from the ever provocative Selma Blair, who experimented with all three looks in under a year. Selma Blair says she works with hairstylists and makeup artists who "have a vision." "I have no fears when it comes to my hair or clothes," proclaims the 36-year-old star of NBC's upcoming mom-and-daughter sitcom "Kath and Kim" and July's action flick "Hellboy II: The Golden Army." Makeup, however, is an entirely different matter for the self-declared "poor applier," who sticks with basics like nude lipstick and pink blush, and ducks whenever she sees a liquid liner. "I avoid anything difficult," she says. Blair's signature look: "A rosy cheek, a smudgy eye, a lot of mascara--I look like a doll that has too much makeup on, and I love it!" Have you always been a beauty chameleon? In high school I would mess with my hair and makeup all the time. I used to wear a shirt that said "Ms. Clairol" because I changed my hair color so much. I was blond for a long time, then what my mom called "barnyard red." Do you still dye it yourself? Only when I have to cover up stray grays. And I'll just use whatever color I find in the grocery store that looks good on the box, like Preference by L'Oréal--because I'm worth it [laughs]. But for my platinum hair, I went to Sheri at Román Salon in L.A. She was a saint. I had just dyed my hair dark brown, so she had to very slowly strip out all the color so that my hair wouldn't burn off. And the cut--are you keeping it short? I tend to like my hair whatever way it's not, so now I miss it being long. I think I'm more approachable with long hair. When it's short, I come across as being artsy and weird. What's your typical makeup look? I used to wear a lot of red lipstick, and when I got a pimple, I'd cover it up with eyeliner to turn it into a beauty mark. But everything has changed since I hit 35. I'm at an age where any makeup that's meant to look "slept in" really looks like I slept in it. That's for youngsters! Now less is more. I don't like to wear concealer or anything. I'd rather have uneven skin than feel like my face is cracking from too much foundation. Then you must be serious about your skin care. I go to a spa in L.A. called Kinara for its Skin Care BootCamp. You go once a week for 12 sessions and they'll look at your skin and tell you how to get it in better condition. They really helped me a lot. I also stay out of the sun. Any thoughts on Botox or plastic surgery? I wanted to get Botox once to make me feel younger. But I don't really have [enough wrinkles] to justify it yet. As for going under the knife, I can't say I wouldn't, but I haven't thought too much about it. Best beauty product? Egyptian Magic cream is my saving grace for everything. It works for my friend's baby's bottom, and I can also use it instead of Chapstick. So what's next? I'm really excited about having a perma-tan and wearing long highlighted hair extensions for my role on "Kath and Kim." And I've been gaining weight for the part by eating a little bit more of what I want and not moving around as much. I've already put on 15 pounds, and I'll probably gain another 10. It'll be a whole new me! Will this be your most drastic transformation? Actually I wore huge prosthetic boobs for a John Waters movie. They were glued on every day by a really handsome guy, but ripping them off every night was definitely outside my realm of comfort. After those bosoms, I didn't mind being flat-chested anymore! outputs.L1:
**(InStyle.com)** — It takes a truly adventurous actress to pull off a razored Mohawk, a platinum pixie, and a Louise Brooks bob. But we’d expect nothing less from the ever-provocative Selma Blair, who experimented with all three looks in less than a year.

Blair says she works with hairstylists and makeup artists who “have a vision.”

“I have no fears when it comes to my hair or clothes,” proclaims the 36-year-old star of NBC’s upcoming mother-daughter sitcom *Kath and Kim* and July’s action film *Hellboy II: The Golden Army*.

Makeup, however, is an entirely different matter for the self-described “poor applier,” who sticks to basics such as nude lipstick and pink blush—and ducks whenever she sees liquid liner.

“I avoid anything difficult,” she says.

Blair’s signature look? “A rosy cheek, a smudgy eye, a lot of mascara—I look like a doll that has too much makeup on, and I love it!”

**Have you always been a beauty chameleon?**

In high school, I would experiment with my hair and makeup all the time. I used to wear a shirt that said “Ms. Clairol” because I changed my hair color so often. I was blond for a long time, then what my mom called “barnyard red.”

**Do you still dye it yourself?**

Only when I have to cover stray grays. I’ll just use whatever color I find in the grocery store that looks good on the box, like Preference by L’Oréal—because I’m worth it [laughs].

But for my platinum hair, I went to Sheri at Román Salon in L.A. She was a saint. I had just dyed my hair dark brown, so she had to strip out all the color very slowly to keep my hair from burning off.

**And the cut—are you keeping it short?**

I tend to like my hair whichever way it isn’t, so now I miss having it long. I think I’m more approachable with long hair. When it’s short, I come across as artsy and weird.

**What’s your typical makeup look?**

I used to wear a lot of red lipstick, and when I got a pimple, I’d cover it with eyeliner and turn it into a beauty mark. But everything has changed since I turned 35. I’m at an age when any makeup meant to look “slept in” really looks as though I slept in it. That’s for youngsters!

Now, less is more. I don’t like wearing concealer or anything like that. I’d rather have uneven skin than feel as though my face is cracking from too much foundation.

**Then you must be serious about skin care.**

I go to a spa in L.A. called Kinara for its Skin Care BootCamp. You go once a week for 12 sessions, and they examine your skin and tell you how to improve its condition. They really helped me a lot. I also stay out of the sun.

**Any thoughts on Botox or plastic surgery?**

I once wanted to get Botox to make me feel younger, but I don’t really have [enough wrinkles] to justify it yet. As for going under the knife, I can’t say I wouldn’t, but I haven’t thought too much about it.

**Best beauty product?**

Egyptian Magic cream is my saving grace for everything. It works on my friend’s baby’s bottom, and I can also use it instead of Chapstick.

**So, what’s next?**

I’m really excited about having a perma-tan and wearing long, highlighted hair extensions for my role on *Kath and Kim*. I’ve also been gaining weight for the part by eating a little more of what I want and not moving around as much. I’ve already put on 15 pounds, and I’ll probably gain another 10. It’ll be a whole new me!

**Will this be your most drastic transformation?**

Actually, I wore huge prosthetic boobs for a John Waters movie. They were glued on every day by a really handsome guy, but ripping them off every night was definitely outside my comfort zone. After those bosoms, I didn’t mind being flat-chested anymore!

outputs.L2:
**(InStyle.com)** — In less than 12 months, Selma Blair tried three dramatically different hairstyles: a shaved Mohawk, a platinum-blond pixie cut, and a bob reminiscent of Louise Brooks. Such bold experimentation suits the famously daring actress, who says she chooses hairstylists and makeup professionals with a strong creative point of view.

Blair, 36, says she is fearless about fashion and hair. She will soon appear in NBC’s mother-daughter comedy *Kath and Kim* and in the July action movie *Hellboy II: The Golden Army*. Applying makeup herself is another story. Describing herself as unskilled at it, she favors simple products such as neutral lipstick and rosy blush and avoids liquid eyeliner or anything else that seems complicated.

Her trademark face consists of pink cheeks, softly smeared eye makeup, and plenty of mascara. She enjoys the resulting effect, which she compares to an overly made-up doll.

**Were you always willing to reinvent your appearance?**

Blair says she constantly played around with cosmetics and hairstyles in high school. Because she dyed her hair so frequently, she even wore a shirt bearing the words “Ms. Clairol.” For a long period she was blond; afterward, she adopted a shade her mother described as “barnyard red.”

**Do you continue to color your own hair?**

She does so only when she needs to hide an occasional gray strand. In those cases, she picks whichever grocery-store dye has the most appealing package—sometimes L’Oréal Preference—jokingly invoking the brand’s “because I’m worth it” slogan.

For her platinum shade, however, she relied on Sheri at Román Salon in Los Angeles. Blair had only recently colored her hair dark brown, so Sheri had to remove the pigment gradually to prevent serious damage. Blair calls her a saint for handling the difficult process.

**Will you keep the short haircut?**

Blair tends to want whichever hairstyle she does not currently have, so she now longs for longer hair. She believes she seems friendlier and more accessible with length, while a short style makes her appear artistic and unusual.

**What makeup do you usually wear?**

In the past, Blair often chose bright red lipstick. If she developed a blemish, she would use eyeliner to disguise it as a beauty mark. Her attitude shifted after she turned 35. She says deliberately rumpled, “slept-in” makeup now looks as though she genuinely forgot to remove it overnight—a style she thinks is better suited to younger people.

These days, she believes restraint is preferable. She avoids concealer and similar coverage products, choosing uneven skin over the tight, cracked sensation caused by excessive foundation.

**Does that mean skin care is especially important to you?**

Blair visits Kinara, a Los Angeles spa, for its Skin Care BootCamp. The program involves one appointment per week for 12 weeks. Specialists evaluate the client’s complexion and recommend ways to improve its condition. Blair says the treatment helped her considerably. She also limits her exposure to sunlight.

**How do you feel about Botox and cosmetic surgery?**

At one point, Blair considered Botox because she hoped it would make her feel younger. She decided she did not yet have enough wrinkles to warrant it. She cannot promise she would never undergo plastic surgery, although she has not given the possibility much consideration.

**Which beauty product does she value most?**

Her essential multipurpose item is Egyptian Magic cream. She says it works on her friend’s baby’s bottom and can also replace Chapstick for her own lips.

**What transformation is coming next?**

For her part in *Kath and Kim*, Blair is enthusiastic about sporting a permanent-looking tan and long, highlighted hair extensions. She is also putting on weight for the role by eating slightly more of the foods she enjoys and reducing her physical activity. She has already gained 15 pounds and expects to add approximately 10 more, creating what she describes as an entirely new version of herself.

**Will that be her biggest physical change for a role?**

Not necessarily. For a John Waters film, Blair wore enormous prosthetic breasts. A very attractive man glued them onto her body each day, but removing them every evening was extremely uncomfortable. After that experience, she says she became perfectly content with having a small chest.

Readers were invited to click for a free trial issue of *InStyle*.

Copyright © 2008 Time Inc. All rights reserved.
outputs.L3:
Selma Blair has long been a fearless beauty chameleon, willing to experiment with dramatic new looks. In less than a year, she moved from a razored Mohawk to a platinum pixie and then to a sleek Louise Brooks–inspired bob. Her adventurous approach extends beyond her hair: Blair also embraces bold clothing and beauty choices, often collaborating with hairstylists and makeup artists who bring a strong creative vision to their work.

Despite her striking red-carpet appearances, Blair does not consider herself particularly skilled at applying makeup. Left to her own devices, she prefers a simple routine built around a few reliable products, including nude lipstick, pink blush, mascara, and softly smudged eye makeup. Since turning 35, her beauty preferences have become increasingly streamlined, with an emphasis on ease rather than elaborate application.

Her willingness to experiment with hair color dates back to high school. She still occasionally reaches for drugstore dye, although more demanding transformations require professional care. Her platinum shade, for example, was created meticulously at a salon to achieve the desired effect while protecting her hair.

Blair appreciates the artistic, edgy quality of short hair and the freedom it gives her to reinvent herself. At the same time, she sometimes misses the warmth and approachability she associates with longer styles. This balance between daring experimentation and simple, accessible beauty defines her distinctive personal style.
outputs.L4:
Selma Blair has never been afraid to take risks with her hair. Over the years, the actress has experimented with dramatic cuts, bold colors, and frequently changing styles, treating her hair as a playful form of self-expression. Although she is open to almost anything, she prefers to leave major transformations to trusted professionals rather than attempting them herself.

Her approach to makeup is much more restrained. When applying it on her own, Blair favors an uncomplicated routine built around rosy cheeks and softly smudged eyes. The familiar look provides a sense of continuity even as her hairstyle shifts from one striking incarnation to another.

Blair also acknowledges that her beauty preferences have evolved since turning 35. Rather than following a fixed formula, she has become more attentive to what feels flattering and authentic at each stage of her life. The contrast between her adventurous hair choices and her consistent makeup reflects a style that is both fearless and grounded: she embraces reinvention while holding on to the elements that make her feel most like herself.
